paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas Hargo took place in Columbus, Ohio, on or shortly before September 15, 1903, when a crowd of about five hundred people chased Hargo, a Black man, through the streets and produced a rope. Police arrived before he was hanged, and Hargo survived with bruises from thrown bricks. The only report found, a short Ohio news brief, gave as the reason that he had beaten his wife, whom it described as a white woman.

According to the brief, "five hundred angry citizens" chased Hargo, "a colored man," for several blocks "because he beat a white woman, his wife." The crowd caught him, a rope was brought out, and the paper wrote that he "was in danger of being lynched." Before police reached the scene, bystanders knocked him down and he was "bruised by a shower of bricks." The "timely arrival of the police," the brief said, saved him from serious injury.
The coverage does not show whether Hargo was arrested or charged, or whether anyone in the crowd was arrested.

The Ohio Democrat of Logan printed the story on September 24 as a Columbus item datelined September 15, under the headline "Police Averted Lynching," in a column of state news briefs between items on a militia regiment and a legislator's death. The brief credited the police, referred to Hargo as "the fellow," and stated the wife-beating as fact rather than as a charge. No Columbus paper, wire version or Black-press account of the episode was found, and no later report followed it.
